title: How Administrators Can Wage War on Bad PD
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Addressed to administrators and PD committees, Stuart argues that bad professional development is driving teachers crazy and lays out how to run and buy better PD. His basics are that whoever is doing the talking is doing the thinking, so PD must mix presenter talk with participant talk, using intentional modes rather than cutesy activities. He describes an inexpensive homegrown model in which coaches film teachers, edit five-to-ten-minute clips and let colleagues rotate through video discussions. For outside consultants he offers five screening questions: is the person in a classroom, do they have quality material online, what do teachers think of them, what results have followed previous workshops, and are they engaging. The tone is conversational and drawn from his experience reading 316 teacher feedback forms.
points: Good PD needs participants talking, not just a presenter delivering content, and each mode of interaction should be chosen with intent rather than for variety's sake.
Homegrown video-visit PD costs about a camera and some editing: coaches film teachers, cut short clips and colleagues discuss them with the host teacher.
Outside PD is valuable at times, for example to calm teachers overwhelmed by earlier Common Core sessions.
Five screening questions help administrators vet consultants, including whether the person is currently teaching and what results their previous workshops produced.
Teachers' skepticism of presenters who are not in classrooms is treated as a real design constraint for PD.
quotes: Whoever's doing the talking is doing the thinking.” Good PD should involve a mixture of a leader talking and participants talking. Any PD that is 100% presented content probably involves someone selling you something and probably won't impact your teachers.
Teachers don't like cutesy, and activity for activity's sake is cutesy.

In my experience, the best homegrown PD involves getting into each others' classrooms and processing what's working and what's not. Yet, due to scheduling and space constraints, this is pretty impractical to do on a large scale.

We watched and discussed three videos that day; it was so refreshing to see teachers we knew doing moves we had learned about. There was nothing flashy, no professional video editing — just teachers watching/discussing teaching.

But it's seriously important to teachers that the person presenting to them understands what it's like to manage a full course load with bloated class sizes and testing pressures and helicopter parents and free/reduced lunch issues and national standards movements.
If the PD person you're looking at has no track record of results to share upon request, your teachers are likely to sense that this person is selling a soft hard-boiled egg.
Some of the brightest researchers and writers in the world are absolutely horrible presenters — just watch a TED talk.
